title: How Daily Blood Pressure Pills Work

lines: Millions of people take a small pill every day to lower their blood pressure.
So how does one tablet calm the push of blood all through your body?
Blood pressure is the push of blood against the walls of your arteries.
It goes up when your heart pumps more blood, when there's more fluid in your blood vessels, or when your arteries get narrower.
Most of these pills work on one of those. Here are four kinds.
First, diuretics, also called water pills, like indapamide.
They help your kidneys get rid of extra salt and water in your urine.
Less fluid in your blood vessels means less push.
Second, ACE inhibitors. Their names often end in pril, like ramipril.
Your body makes a hormone called angiotensin two. It makes blood vessels tighten.
An ACE inhibitor blocks the enzyme that makes it, so your blood vessels relax and get wider.
A common side effect is a dry cough.
Third, ARBs. Their names end in sartan, like losartan.
The hormone is still made, but the pill blocks the spots where it would attach, so it can't tighten your vessels.
If an ACE inhibitor causes a cough, a doctor may switch you to an ARB. But doctors don't combine the two.
Fourth, calcium channel blockers, like amlodipine.
The muscle in your artery walls needs calcium to squeeze.
This pill keeps calcium out of those muscle cells, so the muscle relaxes and the artery widens.
Some people get swollen ankles.
There are others, like beta blockers, which slow your heartbeat. UK guidelines usually keep them for later.
So why every day? Each tablet keeps working for about a day.
So you take the next one before the effect runs out.
These pills control blood pressure, but they don't cure it. If you stop, it can rise back up, even when you feel fine. So never stop without asking your doctor.
And many people need two or more kinds to reach their target.
Which one fits you depends on your age, your ethnic background and your other health conditions.
Talk to your doctor before changing treatment.
